title: No RAGrets
subtitle: M.S. NLP Capstone, Industry-Sponsored Graduate Capstone, Featured by Santa Cruz Works
description:
I led the build of a tool that pulls findings out of scientific papers, links them in a knowledge graph, and traces every answer back to its source. Built with CarbonBridge, a startup that uses microbes to turn methane into methanol.
CarbonBridge's researchers were annotating papers by hand to keep up with their field. I sat with them to learn how they actually read, then led the build around that, from parsing messy PDFs to the graph view where they explore what each paper found. We handed it off fully documented so their team can keep building on it.
details:
- Developed an open-source pipeline for extracting entities, relationships, and technical concepts from scientific literature
- Integrated Docling and Qwen vision-language models for document parsing and information extraction
- Built a React-based interface for graph exploration and AI-assisted literature review
- Set up FastAPI, Dgraph, and containerized infrastructure to support continued use and future development
- Documented architecture and technical decisions to enable project handoff to future contributors

title: HomeHelper
description:
A multi-agent assistant that helps people fix their home appliances, built by a six-person team with an industry sponsor. The code is private, but I'm happy to walk through the architecture.
You show it the broken appliance and talk it through, and it walks you through the repair. I built the agent that coordinates the others, the one that checks their answers, and the part that watches your video and listens to you.
details:
- Built the orchestrator, the Critic agent, and a synthetic self-practice environment that used repair corpora to improve the system through automated feedback
- Built the video and image agent with a 4-bit vision-language model, Whisper transcription, and three-level caching
- Built the React and WebSocket interface

title: SLAC Accelerator Fault Investigator
description:
AI agents that investigate glitches in the machines that power SLAC's particle accelerator, each one reading only its own slice of real data. Built at the Flower agent hackathon at Stanford.
Each agent stays with its own instruments and shares only a short summary, then a lead agent tells a human whether the beam was hit and what caused it. I wrote the plan our team's coding agents built from, and I keep the live demo running so you can replay a real investigation.
details:
- Three agents each hold their own slice of instrument data and send back only a summary, so under 1 percent of the raw data gets shared
- An orchestrator combines the summaries into a verdict for a human, and no tool can touch the equipment
- I wrote the spec and the GitHub issues the team's coding agents built from
- After the event I hosted the live demo from my fork so it stays up for free

title: EduMUSE
description:
An AI study tool that turns course materials into interactive learning, with several agents working together to generate and adapt the content.
Drop in a PDF and it pulls out the key concepts, writes summaries and quizzes, and can even turn the material into a podcast you can listen to.
details:
- Designed specialized agents for concept extraction, summarization, and quiz generation
- Built a modular pipeline for comparing web search, LLM synthesis, and hybrid retrieval approaches
- Developed a React-based interface with PDF upload, text selection, and real-time content generation
- Integrated Flask-based backend services and PDF tooling to support downloadable assessments and summaries
- Extended the system with podcast-style audio generation to support multimodal learning

title: UCSC RAG Chatbot
description:
Team project. Built a retrieval-augmented chatbot to answer questions about the UCSC NLP Master's Program and related university services.
Ask it anything about the NLP master's program and it answers from UCSC's own pages, with a second model checking each answer before you see it. Human graders rated 97 percent of its answers correct, and it shipped as an iOS app.
details:
- Built a RAG pipeline using LangChain, ChromaDB, and LLaMA 3.2 over 77 scraped UCSC-affiliated web pages
- Integrated Gemini 2.0 Flash as a post-response evaluator to check relevance, coherence, and bias before surfacing answers
- Developed a Swift-based iOS app with Firebase for authentication, chat history, and real-time access
- Evaluated the system on a custom 150-question benchmark, achieving 97% human-evaluated accuracy and 71% strict accuracy under Gemini-based evaluation
- Compared performance across three LLaMA model sizes (1B, 3B, and 8B)

title: Personal Portfolio
description:
This site, plus a chat widget that answers questions about my work from the same data you're reading.
The chat runs on a Cloudflare Worker and only pulls in the parts of my background your question is about. The page also builds a plain HTML copy so search engines and resume screeners can read everything.
details:
- Built and deployed a responsive web portfolio to highlight projects, experience, and technical skills
- Designed for smooth navigation and consistent UX across desktop and mobile devices
- Added interactive elements including a dynamic photo gallery and direct links to live projects and repositories
- Used the site as an evolving hub for presenting both technical work and creative interests

title: local-agent-bench
description:
Can a model small enough to run on a laptop drive a real agent? I ran five open models through the same research tasks, and only one reliably finished them.
Most models stalled at the same step, searching the web and then never opening the page that had the answer. gpt-oss 20B was the one that kept going, and the whole benchmark runs locally for free.
details:
- gpt-oss 20B passed 43 of 45 runs. Most of the others stalled at the same step, searching but never opening the page to read the answer
- Every model resisted the prompt injection tasks, though only some went on to finish them
- Tested whether one extra hint sentence in each tool description helps. It helped some models and hurt others
- Fully local and free to run, and the results table is generated straight from the run logs

title: team-build
description:
A Claude Code and Codex plugin that keeps a team's coding agents in sync on one repo, so one person's discovery reaches everyone else's agent.
I built it after a hackathon where we kept redoing each other's work. The team's decisions, the contracts between each person's parts, and who owns what all live in the repo, so every agent starts from the same page.
details:
- Shared decisions, API contracts and the team roster live in repo files that every agent reads
- A simple routine picks one integrator, runs spikes before the work is split, and merges often
- Hooks and a sync check work in both Claude Code and Codex

title: Sentinel: Cyber Incident Response Council
description:
A council of local AI agents that investigates a cyber attack, argues over the response, and asks a human before any big call. Built at the UCSC AI Hackathon and run on one ASUS GX10 with no cloud calls.
I built the Compliance agent, which knows which breach laws an attack triggers and how long the company has to report. It also blocks any move that would destroy evidence the company is legally required to keep.
details:
- I built the Compliance agent, which works out which breach notification rules an incident triggers (GDPR, SEC, HIPAA, NIS2 and others) and how long is left on each deadline
- The model judges and Python counts. Deadlines and the hard rules for escalating to a human are computed in code, not left to the model
- It vetoes destructive actions under a legal hold on any host whose evidence has not been preserved yet
- Passed 21 of 21 ATT&CK-based cases and 25 of 25 cases modeled on public breaches with gemma4 26B, picked after sweeping other local models on the same cases

title: StockPulse
description:
A live stock app that puts price trends and crowd sentiment on the same chart.
It flags the days when the crowd and the price disagree. It runs on AWS for free and watches its own usage, switching itself off before it can cost me anything.
details:
- Candlestick charts with 20 and 50 day moving averages, plus markers on the days where sentiment and price agree or split
- gpt-oss 20B on Groq scores sentiment from Reddit, ApeWisdom and news feeds
- Runs on AWS Lambda as a container image, with DynamoDB for the cache and history and the API key in SSM. Every AWS resource is defined in Terraform
- GitHub Actions deploys each merge to main, logging in to AWS through OIDC so no AWS keys are stored
- Stays inside AWS's free tier: the app tracks its own usage and switches itself off at 80% of the free allowance. Per IP rate limits and a daily cap on model calls protect the Groq key

title: Component Kits
description:
Four small open source libraries I pulled out of code I kept rewriting across projects.
LLM calls, a chat UI, a GitHub client and a disk cache, each one tested and now used across my other projects.
details:
- llm-kit, LLM calls for Ollama and OpenAI compatible APIs plus JSON reply parsing, in TypeScript and Python
- chat-ui, a React chat hook and panel with streaming and abort
- gh-graphql, a GitHub GraphQL client with retries, rate limit waits and resumable paging
- http-cache, a disk cached HTTP GET with atomic writes
- Each one has tests, and my other projects now use them

title: Ranked AI League
description:
Built a browser soccer game with an AI-managed ranked ladder, where every match is simulated on the server so ranked results stay consistent.
Players climb a ranked ladder and nobody can fake a result. The game runs on GitHub Pages, and the league now runs on my own home server.
details:
- Built magic-link sign in and per-player data rules
- Kept one shared simulation engine so every ranked match is computed the same way on the server
- Moved the league off its hosted backend onto my own home server in November 2026
- Personal project

title: repo-impact
description:
Point it at any GitHub repo and get a one-page dashboard of who moves the work forward, instead of who ships the most PRs.
PR counts and lines of code score zero. Real reviews and work on shared code count instead, and every number opens the math behind it. On PostHog, 41 percent of merged PRs over two weeks were approved only by a bot.
details:
- PR count, commit count and lines changed score zero. Substantive reviews, changes to files other engineers also work in, and human-reviewed work count instead
- Fetches every merged PR in the window one day at a time, so GitHub's 1,000 result search cap never drops any, and checks the counts match
- Bots are left out of the scoring and the page reports how much review was automated. On PostHog over two weeks, 41 percent of merged PRs had only a bot approval
- Every number on the page opens the formula and inputs behind it

title: self-healing-scraper
description:
A scraper that asks an LLM to write its CSS selectors once, then stays off the LLM until a site changes.
Normal runs make zero model calls. When a site changes, it repairs only the field that broke and keeps the fix only if it passes the same checks as before.
details:
- Normal runs use the saved selectors and make zero model calls
- When a field breaks, only that field gets repaired, and the new selector is kept only if it passes the same checks as the old one
- A per-run call budget caps model spend
- The demo and tests run offline on saved pages with a recorded model answer, so no key or network is needed

title: policy-tree
description:
Insurers judge prior authorization requests against criteria written as prose. This turns their medical policy PDFs into rule trees that people can read and code can check.
An LLM turns each policy's criteria into rules, and any policy that fails is kept with its error so nothing quietly disappears. It works with OpenAI or a local model.
details:
- Crawls a policy listing page, downloads each PDF, and cuts out the initial criteria section
- An LLM turns the criteria into nested AND/OR rules, validated against a pydantic schema, with one retry that includes the validation error
- Failed policies are stored with their error so they show up in the browser UI instead of disappearing
- Works with OpenAI or any compatible server, including a local Ollama model, and the 33 tests run offline

title: Transformer language model on Penn Treebank
description:
I built a transformer language model with my own attention layers and trained it on the Penn Treebank for my NLP master's.
The smaller tuned model won. It cut test perplexity from 83.35 to 39.11, and the larger model got worse at 134.72.

title: Transformer QA: robustness and domain adaptation

results.metric: Test F1 on COVID-QA, higher is better

description:
I tested how a RoBERTa model trained on SQuAD 2.0 holds up on tricky and out of domain questions, then adapted it to COVID research papers.
Fine tuning it with LoRA on COVID-QA raised test F1 from 43.79 to 54.33 without retraining the whole model.

title: Neural machine translation, French to English
description:
I trained Transformer and CNN models with Fairseq to translate French to English, once with words split into BPE subword pieces and once with whole words.
Whole words won for both models, and the Transformer went from 28.19 to 32.82 BLEU on the test set.
